title: TCS Just Beat Estimates and Crossed $2.6 Billion in AI Revenue. Its Order Book Tells a Different Story.
excerpt: India's largest IT exporter posted a 14 per cent revenue jump and hired 9,300 people — its best quarter in three years. But strip out the rupee's slide, and growth is barely 3 per cent. For 200,000 Indian tech workers in America, the mixed signals matter.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • TCS reported a 14% revenue increase, reaching $7.58 billion in Q1.
  • AI revenue surpassed $2.6 billion, indicating strong growth in AI services.
  • TCS hired 9,300 employees, its highest addition in over three years.
  • The order book shrank to $9.5 billion, raising concerns about future growth.
  • The rupee's decline inflated revenue figures, masking underlying growth challenges.

TCS Q1 Earnings Report
India's largest software exporter has beaten Wall Street's expectations — but the celebration comes with caveats that every Indian tech worker in America should understand. Tata Consultancy Services reported first-quarter revenue of 722.75 billion rupees ($7.58 billion), a 14 per cent jump year-over-year that topped the consensus estimate of 720.30 billion rupees. Net profit rose 4.6 per cent to 133.49 billion rupees, despite a one-time charge from settling an intellectual property theft case with DXC Technology. The results, released Thursday, make TCS the first bellwether for India's $315 billion IT sector to report this earnings season. What it reveals is a sector navigating between two realities: strong headline numbers boosted by a weak rupee, and an underlying business being reshaped by artificial intelligence. ## The AI Number That Matters TCS's annualised AI revenue crossed $2.6 billion, up from $2.3 billion in the previous quarter, driven by faster deployments across industries. That acceleration is the clearest signal yet that India's IT giants are finding real revenue in AI services — not just talking about them. But the number cuts both ways. The same AI tools TCS deploys for clients are the ones analysts say will eventually cannibalise the traditional, labour-intensive model that built India's IT industry. TCS Chairman N. Chandrasekaran has said the "day is not far" when the company would have an equal number of AI agents and employees. > **"Chandrasekaran has said the "day is not far" when the company would have an equal number of AI agents and employees."** ## Hiring Resumes, Order Book Shrinks In a move that defied the industry's grim hiring narrative, TCS added approximately 9,300 employees in the quarter — its highest net addition in more than three years. The hiring came even as broader concerns about AI-driven job losses have pounded the Nifty IT index, which shed 9.5 per cent in the June quarter while the benchmark Nifty 50 gained 6.9 per cent. IT constituents have collectively lost $100 billion in market capitalisation since February. ![Wall Street — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Wall_Street_%2855314253740%29.jpg/3840px-Wall_Street_%2855314253740%29.jpg) The order book, however, shrank to $9.5 billion from $12 billion in the previous quarter, even as TCS announced deals with European manufacturing giant SKF, insurer Canada Life, and Norwegian packaging firm Elopak. Two mega deals in the banking, financial services, and insurance sector from the previous fiscal year helped drive a 2.4 per cent rise in revenue from that critical vertical. ## The Rupee Effect
AI Revenue Growth at TCS
›AI revenue crossed $2.6 billion, up from $2.3 billion.
›Faster AI deployments across industries driving growth.
›AI tools may threaten traditional labor-intensive roles.
›Chairman predicts equal number of AI agents and employees soon.
Much of the headline growth came from currency tailwinds. The rupee's slide — it hit a record low of 96.96 per dollar in May before recovering modestly — flatters rupee-denominated revenues for IT firms that bill in dollars and euros but pay most costs in rupees. Strip out exchange rate effects, and analysts estimate the sector's revenue growth at a mere 2.8 per cent in constant-currency terms. Citi expects a fourth straight year of subdued growth for Indian IT firms. JPMorgan sees revenue growth staying below 3 to 4 per cent for the "foreseeable future." Nomura has called the environment a "perfect storm," with Middle East conflict-led uncertainty compounding AI-driven pricing pressure. ## What It Means for the Diaspora For the estimated 200,000 Indian IT workers in the United States — many employed by TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and HCLTech — the results carry mixed signals. The hiring uptick suggests TCS still sees value in its workforce model, at least for now. But the shrinking order book and the industry's aggressive pivot toward AI agents raise questions about long-term headcount trajectories. The geopolitical backdrop adds another layer. H-1B approvals for India's top IT firms have slumped nearly 40 per cent this year under tighter Trump administration visa rules, pushing companies to hire more locally in the US and move work offshore to India. For Indian professionals on H-1B visas at these firms, the squeeze is coming from both sides: an AI transition that could reduce demand for traditional roles, and an immigration environment that makes staying in America harder.
Impact of the Rupee's Slide
›Rupee hit a record low of 96.96 per dollar.
›Currency effects inflated revenue growth to 14%.
›Constant-currency growth estimated at only 2.8%.
›Analysts predict subdued growth for Indian IT firms.
"This is a marginally better performance from TCS in terms of deal wins and revenue than what we expected, and they have also restarted hiring," said Anshul Jethi, analyst at LKP Securities. "But we need to wait and watch if this is a turnaround or one-off case amid the geopolitical rollercoaster still hurting sentiments." Infosys, HCLTech, and Wipro report later this month. Their numbers will show whether TCS's relative resilience is an industry trend or an outlier.
